title: Feasibility: a test designed to kill the deal
summary: A feasibility study answers four questions in order: who will pay, how fast, against whom, and whether to go. Absorption must be a monthly rate with a required capture rate, competing supply means the whole pipeline, and the go/no-go call is made against kill criteria written before the land money goes hard.
body:
Mr Shabazz, feasibility is not a sales document for the deal. It is a test you design to make the deal fail. If the project survives an honest attempt to kill it, you go; if it does not, you walk away while walking away is still cheap.

Recall

Q. From last week on cycles, why do cap rates tend to drift up when interest rates rise?

A. Because buyers compare a property’s yield with what money costs and with what safer investments pay. When borrowing gets dearer, a buyer needs a higher starting yield to make the purchase work, so they pay less for the same income, which shows up as a higher capitalisation rate (cap rate). The link is real but loose and lagged, not mechanical.

Q. From the law and tax checkpoint, what separates tax avoidance from tax evasion?

A. Avoidance arranges affairs within the law and discloses the facts; evasion hides or misstates facts and is a crime. Avoidance can still fail if an anti-avoidance rule applies, which is why substance matters.

Q. From contracts, does a signed letter of intent bind you to buy the land?

A. Usually not on price and closing if it says it is non-binding and leaves essential terms open. But individual clauses, such as exclusivity, confidentiality and who pays costs, are often drafted to bind. Read each paragraph for the words that make it binding.

Why this matters

Every dollar you spend before construction is a bet on a forecast of demand. Land deposits, design fees, the planning application, the geotechnical report: all of it assumes that, when the building is finished, enough people will rent or buy what you made, at the price you assumed, fast enough to pay the lender. If the forecast is wrong, no amount of good construction saves the project. A building finished on time and on budget into an empty market is still a failure. Feasibility is the cheapest place to find that out.

Four questions, in this order

In plain English, a feasibility study answers four questions. Who will pay for this? How many of them, and how fast? Who else is chasing the same people? And, given the answers, do we go or stop?

The professional framing names them demand, absorption, competing supply and the go/no-go decision. Demand is not population. It is the number of households, buyers or guests who have a reason to choose this location, the income to pay the price, and a trigger to move in the window you care about. A city of 500,000 people says almost nothing. Six hundred renter households a year, earning enough to pay between $1,800 and $2,200 a month, forming or moving within two kilometres of your site, says a great deal. Those figures are hypothetical, and the point is the shape: a demand estimate names a price band, a geography and a time period, or it is not an estimate.

Absorption is a number, not an adjective

Brokers say “absorption is strong.” That sentence cannot be tested, so it cannot be used. You need absorption as a rate. The absorption rate is the number of units leased or sold per month in a defined market. Your project then needs a capture rate: the share of all qualifying demand in that market that your project must win to hit its own schedule.

Worked example one, with hypothetical numbers. Your submarket produces about 600 qualifying renter households a year, which is 50 a month. Your building has 150 units and your financing plan assumes lease-up in 15 months. That is 150 divided by 15, or 10 leases a month. Your required capture rate is 10 divided by 50, which is 20 percent. In words: one in every five qualifying households that moves in this area over the next 15 months must choose your building.

Say that out loud now.

Twenty percent may be reasonable or absurd. That depends entirely on who else is in the market, which is the third question.

Competing supply: count what is coming, not what is open

The beginner counts the buildings that already exist. The professional counts the pipeline: projects under construction, projects approved but not started, and projects with applications filed. Those are the buildings that will open into the same months as yours and chase the same households.

Worked example two, continuing the numbers. Over your 15-month window, three other projects totalling 450 units will deliver. With yours, that is 600 new units chasing 750 qualifying households, which is 15 months times 50. On the surface the market absorbs it. Now apply a fair share test. Your fair share is your units divided by all competing new units: 150 divided by 600, or 25 percent. Your required capture is 20 percent. Required capture below fair share is a pass. Now suppose an approved 300-unit project that had stalled gets financed and starts. New supply becomes 900 units against 750 households, and your fair share drops to 150 divided by 900, about 16.7 percent. Your required 20 percent is now above your fair share. You can still win, but only by being better or cheaper, and your pro forma just assumed neither. That is a fail, unless you change the product, the price or the timeline.

Go or no-go against criteria written in advance

The fourth question is answered with kill criteria: the specific results that stop the project, written and dated before the land money goes hard. Hypothetical examples: stop if required capture exceeds fair share by more than a quarter; stop if pipeline supply in the window exceeds 18 months of demand; stop if the downside case, with lease-up 50 percent slower, cannot carry its interest from equity on hand. These thresholds are judgement calls for you to set, not industry standards. What matters is that you set them before you are in love with the site.

How the best do it

Disciplined institutional developers separate the people who want the deal from the people who test it. Typically an independent market consultant prepares the demand study, an internal reviewer who did not source the deal challenges it, and an investment committee decides against criteria agreed beforehand. What a small developer can copy costs very little: one page of kill criteria signed before the land agreement goes firm, and a consultant whose fee does not change whether you proceed or not.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is motivated reasoning: the feasibility gets written after the decision has emotionally been made, so every assumption bends toward yes. The control is mechanical. Kill criteria are written first. The person testing demand is not the person who found the site. And any change to the criteria after you see the results is recorded with the reason, so you can see yourself moving the goalposts.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner uses total population or a broker’s adjective as demand, counts only buildings already open as competition, and treats the absorption assumption as a single number with no downside case. Then the financing is sized on that number, and the first slow month becomes a cash problem.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: money spent on feasibility for a project you later abandon may be treated differently from costs of a project you build; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a study you share can invite reliance by others, so label who it is for. Banking: your lender will commission its own view and usually slow your absorption; size the deal to their number, not yours. Governance: decide who has authority to call go or no-go, and minute the decision. Estate: options, deposits and pursuit costs are assets and obligations your executors would need to understand, so keep a register. Exit: the buyer you sell to will underwrite the same competing supply, so your exit price depends on this work too.

Callback

In Week 2 you met the outside view: before trusting your own forecast, ask how similar projects actually performed. Absorption is the outside view made concrete. The leasing history of the last five buildings that opened in your submarket is your reference class, and it outranks any projection, including your own. Last week’s cycle lessons add the timing layer: a pipeline that looks safe today can double when credit loosens.

Recap

Feasibility answers four questions in order: who will pay, how fast, against whom, and do we go. Absorption becomes a monthly rate and a required capture rate. Competing supply means the pipeline, tested against your fair share. And the decision is made against kill criteria written before you were committed.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics — Dubai in 2009, where sales were mistaken for demand.
checklist: Write demand as a price band, a geography and a time period, never as population.
Convert absorption into units per month and a required capture rate.
List the competing pipeline: under construction, approved and applied, with delivery dates.
Run the fair share test: required capture against your share of new supply.
Write and date kill criteria before the land deposit goes hard.
Give the demand test to someone who did not source the deal.
Record any change to the criteria after you see results, with the reason.
head: Field checklist
speak: Feasibility is a test I design to kill the deal. It answers four questions in order. Who will pay: households with a reason, an income and a trigger, in a named price band and area. How fast: absorption as units per month, and the capture rate my schedule demands. On hypothetical numbers, 150 units in 15 months is 10 a month; if the area produces 50 qualifying households a month, I need one in five. Against whom: the whole pipeline, not just what is open. If 600 new units chase 750 households, my fair share is 25 percent and I need 20, so I pass. If a stalled 300-unit project restarts, my fair share falls below what I need, and I fail unless I change the product, the price or the timing. Finally, go or no-go, against kill criteria I signed before the land money went hard, tested by someone who did not find the site.
terms: Absorption rate — the number of units leased or sold per month in a defined market.
Capture rate — the share of all qualifying demand in a market that a project must win to meet its own schedule.
Competing supply pipeline — every project under construction, approved or applied for that will deliver into the same market window.

hostile.q: Your study says the market absorbs 50 units a month. Where does that number come from, and what happens to my loan if it is 30?
hostile.a: It comes from household formation and moves in a named rent band and area, checked against how the last five comparable buildings actually leased. At 30 a month my required capture rises from 20 to about 33 percent, lease-up stretches by roughly two-thirds, and the downside case shows the extra interest is carried from equity already committed, before your loan is touched.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman assisting on finance
title: Dubai 2009: when sales were mistaken for demand
summary: Dubai’s boom sold large volumes of units off-plan, many to investors intending to resell before completion, while long projects were funded with short-term borrowing. When credit froze in 2008 resale demand vanished, and on 25 November 2009 Dubai World asked creditors to pause repayments. The root cause was absorption measured by contract rather than by occupancy.
body:
Mr Shabazz, Dubai’s property crash of 2008 and 2009 is a lesson in one confusion: sales were counted as demand. When most buyers intend to resell before completion, the market is measuring appetite for a price rise, not appetite for a home, and that appetite vanishes the moment credit does.

Recall

Q. From last week, what usually turns a property cycle down?

A. Supply delivered on the optimism of the boom arrives just as credit tightens or demand slows. Projects started at the peak complete into the downturn, because buildings take years and money changes in months.

Q. From the law and tax checkpoint, what does “substance over form” mean?

A. That a tax authority or court may look at what a transaction really does, rather than how it is labelled. A transaction dressed as one thing but functioning as another can be taxed on its function.

Q. From contracts, what is the difference between a condition and a warranty?

A. A condition is a term so important that breaking it can let the other side end the contract; a warranty is a lesser term whose breach usually gives a right to damages only. Many modern contracts define their own consequences instead of relying on the labels.

Why this matters

Ford here, with Roman assisting on the finance. You will sell or lease into markets where other people’s money is moving fast. When you sell units before completion, early sales feel like proof. This case teaches you to ask who the buyers are and why they bought, because the answer decides whether your sales survive a change in credit. We take it through seven steps: timeline, key decisions, assumptions, incentives, warning signs ignored, point of no return and root cause. This lesson sticks to the broad public record; where details are contested we say so.

Step 1: Timeline

In the early 2000s Dubai opened designated areas to freehold ownership by foreigners. A construction boom followed, with large master-planned communities, artificial islands and towers, much of it led by companies connected to the government, including Nakheel, part of the Dubai World group. Many units were sold off-plan, meaning before or during construction, often with deposits that were small relative to the price. Prices rose fast through 2007 and into 2008. When the global financial crisis tightened credit in late 2008, transactions dried up and prices fell steeply. On 25 November 2009, Dubai World announced it would ask creditors to pause repayments on its debts. A Nakheel Islamic bond due in December 2009 was repaid after support from Abu Dhabi, and Dubai World negotiated a restructuring of its bank debt during 2010. Many projects stalled or were cancelled.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Launching very large projects at the same time, across many developers. Funding long construction with borrowing that came due much sooner than the projects could produce cash. And selling off-plan on terms that made it easy to buy with a small deposit and resell before completion.

Step 3: Assumptions

The core assumption was that sales velocity showed demand. A project that sold out its first phase in days seemed to prove the market wanted more. But a large share of buyers were investors intending to resell the purchase contract before completion, a practice called flipping. The second assumption was that credit would keep rolling over. The third was that prices would keep rising long enough for each layer of buyers to exit.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Incentives

Developers were rewarded for launches and sales, because deposits funded construction and showed momentum. Brokers were paid on transactions, including resales of the same unit. Speculators were rewarded by price rises, not by occupancy. Lenders saw rising values as security. No party at the table was paid to ask the plain question: when these towers are finished, who will live in them, and at what rent?

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

Contemporary commentary noted resale activity on uncompleted units and a supply pipeline running far ahead of population growth. Completed buildings could be tested against rents, and rents could not justify the prices being paid for many uncompleted units. Each of those was visible before the crisis. Each was explained away by the next sale.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was not November 2009. It was the period when huge multi-year projects were committed on short-term money. Once that mismatch existed, the projects could only finish if credit and resale buyers kept arriving. When the global credit freeze hit in late 2008, the outcome was largely fixed. The 2009 announcement only made it public.

Step 7: Root cause

Roman’s summary: the root cause was absorption measured by contract, not by occupancy. Demand from end users, the people who will actually live in or use a building, was never separated from demand by investors betting on the price. Funding on short maturities turned that error into a debt crisis rather than just a price correction.

What the feasibility should have asked

Roman again. Put yourself in the seat of a lender reviewing one Dubai tower in 2006. The sales report shows the first phase sold within days. A disciplined lender asks four further questions. What share of buyers intend to occupy? How many contracts have already been assigned to a second buyer? What rent could a completed unit earn, and what does that rent imply as a value? And when does this loan fall due compared with when the building can produce cash? None of those questions requires hindsight. Each was answerable from the documents of the day. A study that answered them would have shown that the market was pricing future resale, not present use, and that the debt depended on resale continuing.

The general lesson is that velocity is a symptom, not a cause. Fast sales can come from genuine shortage or from speculation, and the two look identical in a weekly sales report. They separate only when you look at who is buying and why. That is cheap to find out before launch and very expensive to discover after completion.

The small-project version

This is a composite example. A developer launches 60 condominium units with a 5 percent deposit. Forty sell in a month, which looks excellent. Then a sales agent mentions that half the buyers own several units elsewhere and plan to assign their contracts before closing. When rates rise a year later, assignment buyers disappear, and those investors walk away from their deposits rather than close. On a hypothetical $400,000 unit, a 5 percent deposit is $20,000, so walking away costs the buyer $20,000 and costs the developer the remaining $380,000 of sale that the construction loan assumed. Twenty defaults is $7.6 million of expected proceeds gone, against $400,000 of forfeited deposits. The lender stops funding draws. The early sales were never demand.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting a fast sales start as proof of the feasibility study, instead of as a fact to be tested. The control: classify every pre-sale buyer as an intended occupier or an investor, track the mix, and set a ceiling on investor share and on assignments. Size deposits so that walking away hurts more than closing.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner reports “we sold 70 percent in six weeks” to the lender and stops looking. The professional reports the same figure with the occupier share, the deposit level, and the closing rate on the last comparable project that completed in a downturn.

Callback

In the first lesson of this week, required capture was tested against fair share of the pipeline. Dubai shows the missing layer: the demand you count must be end-user demand, because an investor’s purchase moves the unit, not the household. And in Week 3 you studied loss aversion: buyers who would rather lose a deposit than close at a loss are behaving exactly as that research predicts.

Recap

Dubai’s boom confused sales with demand and funded long projects with short money. When credit froze, resale buyers vanished and the debt came due. Rule 28 follows from it.

Rule 28: Count only end-user demand as absorption; track the investor share of every pre-sale, and never fund a long build with money that comes due before the building can pay it back.

Next: Roman, The Money — what slow absorption does to interest, returns and refinancing.
checklist: Classify every pre-sale buyer as an intended occupier or an investor.
Report the occupier share alongside every sales figure.
Set a ceiling on investor share and on contract assignments before launch.
Size deposits so that walking away costs more than closing.
Match debt maturities to the date the building can actually repay.
Test sales prices against the rents a completed unit can earn.
Run the seven steps on any market failure you study.
head: Field checklist
speak: Dubai opened freehold ownership to foreigners in the early 2000s and a boom followed. Huge projects were launched at once and sold off-plan, often with small deposits, and a large share of buyers planned to resell before completion. Prices rose fast, then the global credit freeze of late 2008 stopped the resale buyers, prices fell steeply, and on 25 November 2009 Dubai World asked its creditors to pause repayments. The point of no return was earlier: committing multi-year projects on short-term money. The root cause was absorption measured by contracts signed rather than by people who would actually live in the buildings. My rule: count only end-user demand as absorption, track the investor share of every pre-sale, and never fund a long build with money that comes due before the building can repay it.
terms: Off-plan sale — a sale of a unit before or during construction, on the basis of plans.
Flipping — buying a unit, or the right to buy it, with the intention of reselling it at a profit before completion.
End-user demand — demand from people who will actually occupy or use the space, as opposed to investors buying for resale.

hostile.q: You have sold 70 percent of the units. Why should I believe those buyers will close?
hostile.a: Because I can show you who they are. The schedule splits buyers into occupiers and investors; investor share is capped by our sales policy, deposits are sized so walking away costs more than closing, and assignments need our consent. I will also show you the closing rate on comparable projects that completed in a falling market.

rule: Rule 28: Count only end-user demand as absorption; track the investor share of every pre-sale, and never fund a long build with money that comes due before the building can pay it back.

title: What slow absorption does to your money
summary: Every extra month of sell-out adds carry and stretches time, so a modest fall in profit becomes a large fall in annual return. On a rental, occupancy on the refinance date sets the size of the take-out loan, and a shortfall becomes a cash call on a fixed date. Size loan terms, extensions and reserves to the slow case.
body:
Mr Shabazz, slow absorption does not just delay profit; it destroys it, because every extra month carries interest and costs while the clock runs on your return. And on a rental, the lease-up on the day your loan matures decides how much new debt you can raise to pay it off.

Recall

Q. From this week’s first lesson, what is a capture rate?

A. The share of all qualifying demand in a market that your project must win to meet its own schedule. Ten leases a month in a market producing 50 qualifying households a month is a 20 percent capture.

Q. From the law and tax checkpoint, what is a general anti-avoidance rule in concept?

A. A broad rule that lets a tax authority deny a tax benefit from a transaction that technically complies with the law but abuses its purpose. The details and tests vary by country; verify against the primary source.

Q. From contracts, what are the usual remedies for breach?

A. Damages to put the injured party where they would have been, and in some cases specific performance, an order to actually do what was promised. Land contracts are a classic setting for specific performance, because land is treated as unique.

Why this matters

Roman here. Lenders read a feasibility study backwards. They do not ask whether you can sell the units; they ask what happens to them if you sell them slowly. Your own returns ride on the same question. If you understand how the absorption assumption flows into interest, return and refinancing, you can design the deal so a slow market costs you time rather than the building.

Carry: the meter that runs while you wait

In plain English, carry is everything that costs money each month while the product is unsold or unleased: loan interest, property tax, insurance, marketing, security and utilities on an empty building. Professionals call this the carry cost and model it month by month, because it grows with every month of sell-out period, the time from first sale to last closing.

Worked example one, hypothetical. A 100-unit condominium sells at an average of $500,000, so gross revenue is $50 million. All-in cost is $40 million, funded by $12 million of equity and a $28 million loan at 8 percent interest. The base case sells out in 12 months after completion and gives a $10 million profit over three years. Now absorption runs at half pace and sell-out takes 24 months. During sell-out the loan is repaid as units close, so on average about half of it, $14 million, is outstanding. Interest on $14 million at 8 percent is about $1.12 million a year, or roughly $93,000 a month. Twelve extra months is about $1.12 million of interest. Add hypothetical marketing and holding costs of $50,000 a month, another $600,000. Profit falls from $10 million to about $8.3 million.

That looks survivable until you add time. With all equity treated as invested at the start, a rough simplification, the base case returns $22 million on $12 million over three years, an equity multiple of 1.83 and an annual return near 22 percent. The slow case returns $20.3 million over four years, a multiple of 1.69 and an annual return near 14 percent. A 17 percent cut in profit became a cut of about a third in the annual return, because the money was tied up a year longer.

Say that out loud now.

Rentals: lease-up meets the refinance

A rental building is usually built with a construction loan that must be repaid by a permanent loan. The permanent lender sizes the new loan on the building’s net operating income (NOI), the rent collected minus operating costs, using a debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), which is NOI divided by the annual loan payments. Coverage levels and loan constants are commercial practice that lenders set deal by deal, not a standard; the figures below are hypothetical.

Worked example two. A 120-unit building is projected to reach stabilised NOI of $1.8 million. The permanent lender requires a DSCR of 1.25 and uses an annual payment constant of 7.5 percent of the loan. Maximum annual payment is $1.8 million divided by 1.25, which is $1.44 million. Divided by 0.075, the maximum loan is $19.2 million, which repays the construction loan. Now lease-up is slow and on the refinance date the building is 70 percent leased. Operating costs are largely fixed, so NOI is only about $1.0 million. Maximum payment is $800,000; maximum loan is about $10.7 million. The gap is $8.5 million, and it is due on the construction loan’s maturity date. You either find that money, negotiate an extension at the lender’s price, or lose the building.

Price or time

When sales slow, a developer has two dials: cut the price to restore the pace, or hold the price and accept the time. Run both before you choose. Using the same hypothetical condominium, a 5 percent price cut across all 100 units costs $2.5 million of revenue. Holding the price and taking 12 extra months cost about $1.7 million of carry, plus the return lost to time. On those numbers, holding looks cheaper in dollars and worse in return. But there is a third effect: a price cut is visible to every buyer who already signed, and some may try to renegotiate or walk away. Holding price protects existing contracts but extends your exposure to the market. Neither answer is always right. The professional move is to compute both in the feasibility, before launch, so the decision in a slow month is made against numbers rather than nerves.

Designing for the slow case

Three design moves protect you. First, size the construction loan term to the slow case, not the base case, so maturity arrives after a realistic stabilisation. Second, negotiate extension options in advance, with conditions you can meet, because an extension you must beg for is priced by the lender. Third, hold an interest and lease-up reserve funded from day one. Each costs something in the base case. Each is cheap compared with an $8.5 million gap.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick’s note for your personal balance sheet. Feasibility risk does not stay inside the project company. If you sign a completion guarantee or a carry guarantee, a slow market becomes a claim on your personal assets, so record every guarantee as a contingent liability. Slow absorption also locks your equity up longer, which lowers your liquidity floor, the cash you keep untouchable. Before you commit equity, ask what your personal balance sheet looks like if this money comes back a year late.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is sizing debt and maturity to the base-case absorption. The control: every loan term, extension and reserve is tested against a downside case with absorption at least a third slower, and the gap at refinance is calculated explicitly.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner models lease-up as one line, assumes the refinance happens on the stabilised number, and never computes the maximum loan at the occupancy actually likely on the maturity date. They also treat carry as a contingency line rather than a schedule, so when sales slow there is no clear picture of how many months the equity can carry before the lender must be asked for help. Build the carry schedule monthly, and mark the month in which committed equity runs out in the downside case. That month is the real deadline on your feasibility.

Callback

In Week 15 you learned that the internal rate of return (IRR) punishes time: the same profit earned a year later is worth less. This lesson shows the mechanism in the field. Absorption is the variable that converts a market slowdown into time, and time is where returns go to die.

Recap

Slow absorption adds carry and stretches time, so a moderate profit cut becomes a large return cut. On a rental, occupancy on the refinance date sizes the take-out loan, and a gap there is a cash call on a fixed date. Design the loan term, extensions and reserves for the slow case.

Next: LEX, The Rules — who may rely on a market study, and what happens when a forecast goes into an investor deck.
checklist: Model carry month by month: interest, tax, insurance, marketing, security, utilities.
Run sell-out or lease-up at least a third slower than base.
Compute the annual return, not just profit, in the slow case.
Calculate the maximum take-out loan at the occupancy likely on the maturity date.
Size the construction loan term to the slow case.
Negotiate extension options with conditions you can meet, before you need them.
Record every guarantee as a contingent liability on your personal balance sheet.
head: Field checklist
speak: Slow absorption hurts twice. First, carry: interest, tax, insurance and marketing keep running every month a unit sits unsold. On a hypothetical 100-unit condo, doubling the sell-out from 12 to 24 months costs about 1.7 million and cuts profit from 10 million to 8.3. Second, time: the annual return falls from about 22 percent to about 14, because the money is tied up a year longer. On a rental the danger is the refinance. The permanent lender sizes the loan on net operating income divided by a required coverage ratio. A building that would support a 19.2 million loan when stabilised might support only about 10.7 million at 70 percent leased, leaving an 8.5 million gap on the construction loan maturity date. So I size the loan term to the slow case, negotiate extensions in advance and hold a lease-up reserve.
terms: Carry cost — the monthly cost of holding an unsold or unleased project, such as interest, tax, insurance and marketing.
Sell-out period — the time from the first sale to the last closing on a for-sale project.
Downside case — a version of the pro forma with deliberately worse assumptions, used to test survival rather than to predict.

hostile.q: Your construction loan matures 12 months after completion. What do you do if you are 70 percent leased on that day?
hostile.a: I will not be in that position by surprise. The term is sized to the slow case, I have two six-month extension options with occupancy tests we can meet, and there is a lease-up reserve. If all of that fails, the gap is calculated in the downside case and covered by committed equity, not by hope.

title: Who may rely on a market study
summary: A market study is professional advice governed first by its engagement letter and, beyond that, by the law of negligent misstatement. Lenders and others rely on it through reliance letters negotiated early. When you pass a forecast to investors or buyers, label it, show the downside and the key assumptions, and have counsel review it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a market study is advice written for someone. Who may rely on it, what the author is liable for, and what happens when you quote it to investors or buyers are legal questions, and the answers are decided by the engagement letter and the way you use the document.

Recall

Q. From this week, what is Rule 28?

A. Count only end-user demand as absorption; track the investor share of every pre-sale, and never fund a long build with money that comes due before the building can pay it back.

Q. From the law and tax checkpoint, what does legal privilege protect, in concept?

A. Certain confidential communications with a lawyer made for legal advice, so they need not be disclosed. Its scope and exceptions vary by jurisdiction, and sharing the advice widely can lose it.

Q. From contracts, what is an exclusion clause?

A. A term that limits or excludes one party’s liability. Courts read such clauses carefully and may refuse to enforce them in some circumstances, so their exact wording matters.

Why this matters

LEX here. You will commission studies, receive studies from brokers and lenders, and put forecasts in front of partners and buyers. Each of those is a legal relationship, even when nobody calls it one. If a forecast is badly wrong, the questions become who owed a duty to whom, who relied on what, and whether the document warned them. Getting this right protects you twice: you can recover from a negligent consultant, and you can avoid being the one who misled an investor.

The duty behind a study

In plain English, the consultant who writes your market study owes you the care a competent professional in that field would take, under their contract with you and often under the law of negligence. The professional framing starts with the contract: the engagement letter sets the scope, the assumptions, the limit on liability and who the report is for. Outside the contract, the law of negligent misstatement can make an adviser liable to someone who relied on careless advice, where the relationship justifies it. The landmark English case is Hedley Byrne v Heller, decided by the House of Lords in 1963, which recognised liability for negligent statements causing financial loss. Common-law courts, including in Canada, have developed the principle since; the exact tests differ, so verify against the primary source before you rely on it.

Worked example one, hypothetical. You commission a study under an engagement letter that says the report is for your use only and caps liability at the fee. Your lender wants to rely on it. If you simply send it, the lender may have no claim against the consultant, and the consultant may resist being exposed to one. The usual solution is a reliance letter: a short agreement in which the consultant permits a named third party, here the lender, to rely on the report, usually on the same terms and limits as the original engagement. You negotiate it before the report is delivered, not after a dispute.

Say that out loud now.

When you pass a forecast on

The second risk runs the other way. When you put absorption or rent forecasts into an investor presentation, a joint venture proposal or a condominium sales document, you are making statements that others may rely on. If a statement of fact is false, or a forecast is presented without a reasonable basis, or a material adverse fact is left out, you may face a claim for misrepresentation, and in the securities context, statutory liability. Forecasts are not forbidden. They are forward-looking statements, and the law in many places treats them more kindly when they are clearly labelled, accompanied by the key assumptions and the main risk factors, and honestly believed when made. The specific rules and protections differ widely; this is concept, not a conclusion for any jurisdiction.

Condominium buyers raise the stakes. Many jurisdictions require a developer to give buyers a formal disclosure document before or at the time of sale, and statements in it about the project, the budget or the timing can carry their own remedies, sometimes including a right for the buyer to cancel. If your sales team repeats absorption or price-growth claims to buyers, those statements can become part of the buyer’s case. Train the team to describe the building, not to predict the market.

Worked example two, hypothetical. Your consultant’s report gives a base case of 12 months to sell out and a downside of 22 months. Your investor deck shows “sell-out projected in 12 months, per independent market study.” The downside is not mentioned. The market slows and sell-out takes 20 months. An investor argues that you selected the favourable half of the study and used the consultant’s name to give it authority. Whether that claim succeeds depends on the law and the facts, but you have handed them the argument. The safer line is the whole picture: the base case, the downside, the main assumptions, and a statement that forecasts may not be achieved. The consultant’s engagement letter may also forbid you from quoting their name in marketing without consent.

Read the limitations section first

Every competent market study ends with a section of assumptions and limiting conditions. Beginners skip it. Professionals read it first, because it tells you what the author refuses to stand behind. Typical items: the author relied on data supplied by others without verifying it; the conclusions assume no material change in economic conditions after the data date; the study does not cover a particular product type or price band. Each of those is fair. Each also shifts risk back to you. If the study assumes stable interest rates and you are financing in a rising market, the conclusion is weaker than its headline. Write the three limitations that matter most to your deal on the front page of your own feasibility memo, so nobody reading the headline misses them.

The same applies to studies you receive from others. When a lender shares its own consultant’s report, or a seller hands you a study prepared for them, you are usually not a party to that engagement and may have no right to rely on it. Treat it as information to test, not as advice you can recover on.

What to put in the engagement letter

Five items carry most of the protection. The scope: which markets, products and price bands. The data sources and the date the data runs to. The named parties who may rely on the report. The liability cap and whether it applies to third parties under a reliance letter. And the permitted uses: internal decision, lender submission, investor disclosure. A consultant asked at the start will price these terms. A consultant asked after a dispute will refuse.

Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the relevant jurisdiction, for the engagement letter, any reliance letter, and any offering or sales document that contains forecasts.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is quoting a study selectively to people who will rely on it. The control: any forecast that leaves your office travels with its downside case, its key assumptions and a forward-looking statement warning, and anything going to investors or buyers is reviewed by counsel first.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner forwards the consultant’s report to the lender and an investor as a courtesy, without a reliance letter and without reading the permitted-use clause. Then, when the forecast fails, nobody can rely on the report and everybody can rely on the developer’s email.

Callback

In Week 20 you learned that a letter of intent can bind in some paragraphs and not others. An engagement letter works the same way for advice: its few lines on reliance and liability decide who can recover when the forecast fails. And in Week 21 you met negligence and agency, the doctrines this lesson applies to the humble market study.

Recap

A market study is professional advice governed by its engagement letter and, outside that, by the law of negligent misstatement. Third parties rely through reliance letters, negotiated early. When you pass forecasts on, label them, give the downside and key assumptions, and have counsel review anything going to investors or buyers.

Next: Sage, The Numbers — reverse engineering the absorption a sell-out date really requires.
checklist: Read the engagement letter for scope, data date, reliance, liability cap and permitted uses.
Negotiate any reliance letter for a lender before the report is delivered.
Never forward a study to a third party as a courtesy without checking permitted use.
Show base case and downside together whenever a forecast leaves your office.
State the key assumptions and a forward-looking statement warning beside every forecast.
Get consent before quoting a consultant’s name in marketing.
Have counsel review any investor or sales document containing forecasts.
head: Field checklist
speak: A market study is professional advice, and the engagement letter decides most of what matters: the scope, the date the data runs to, who may rely on it, the cap on liability and the permitted uses. Beyond the contract, the law of negligent misstatement, recognised in Hedley Byrne in 1963 and developed since, can make an adviser liable to someone who relied on careless advice, but the tests differ by jurisdiction. If my lender wants to rely on my study, I negotiate a reliance letter before delivery. The other risk is mine: when I put a forecast in an investor deck or sales document, I show the base case and the downside, the key assumptions and a clear warning that forecasts may not be achieved. Quoting only the good half, under the consultant’s name, is how a developer turns a slow market into a misrepresentation claim. Counsel reviews anything going to investors or buyers.
terms: Reliance letter — an agreement in which a report’s author permits a named third party to rely on it, usually on the original terms and limits.
Negligent misrepresentation — a careless false statement, relied on by someone to whom a duty was owed, causing them loss.
Forward-looking statement — a forecast or projection about future results, which should be labelled and accompanied by its assumptions and risks.

hostile.q: Your deck says sell-out in 12 months per an independent study. Did the study have a downside case, and why is it not here?
hostile.a: It did: 22 months. You are right that it belongs beside the base case, and the revised deck shows both, the key assumptions and the risk factors, and has been reviewed by our counsel. The consultant has also consented in writing to being named.

title: Reverse engineering the absorption a deal needs
summary: Working backward from the sell-out or lease-up date the financing requires exposes the real assumption: the monthly pace, the capture rate against fair share, the leads and visits per month, and the marketing budget. Break-even absorption, the market rate at which the deal just survives, belongs on the front page.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this lesson starts at the finish line and walks backward. Tell me the sell-out date the deal needs, and I will tell you the monthly pace, the share of the market, and the number of serious buyers you must find each month to get there. Then you can judge whether that is believable.

Recall

Q. From this week, what is the gap at refinance?

A. The difference between the construction loan that must be repaid and the largest permanent loan the building’s actual net operating income can support on the maturity date.

Q. From the law and tax checkpoint, what is the beneficial owner of an asset?

A. The person who ultimately enjoys its benefits and control, as distinct from the person or entity named on title or holding it as nominee.

Q. From contracts, what is an entire agreement clause?

A. A term stating that the written contract is the whole agreement, intended to exclude earlier promises and discussions from forming part of it.

Why this matters

Sage here. Forecasts are easy to inflate going forward: you add a little optimism at each step and the result looks reasonable. Working backward from the outcome you need exposes the assumption you are really making. If the answer is that you need one in four of every buyer in the city, you will see it plainly. This is even-week reverse engineering, and it is the fastest honesty test in development.

Worked example one: a condominium sell-out, backward

All figures are hypothetical. The finished outcome the financing requires is this: 160 units sold within 20 months of launch.

  1. Required pace. 160 units divided by 20 months is 8 units a month.
  2. Market size. Sales of comparable new condominium units in the submarket have averaged 600 a year over the last three years, which is 50 a month. Units: new-unit sales per month, not total transactions, because resales of older units are a different product.
  3. Required capture. 8 divided by 50 is 16 percent of all comparable new-unit sales.
  4. Fair share. Five other projects will be selling during your window, so six in total. If all were equal, each would take one sixth, about 16.7 percent. Your required 16 percent sits just below fair share. That means you need an average product at an average price, and you have no margin for being worse.
  5. Sales funnel. Your sales consultant reports, from comparable launches, that about 15 percent of people who visit the sales centre sign a contract, and about 2 percent of web or phone enquiries, called leads, become a contract. Required visits: 8 divided by 0.15 is about 53 a month. Required leads: 8 divided by 0.02 is 400 a month.
  6. Marketing budget. If a lead costs about $100 to generate, 400 leads cost $40,000 a month, or $800,000 over 20 months. Check that the pro forma carries it.

Now ask the honest question at each line. Is 50 a month a stable market, or the top of a cycle? Is the conversion rate from a strong market or a weak one? If the market falls to 35 a month, required capture becomes 8 divided by 35, about 23 percent, well above fair share. The backward calculation tells you exactly which assumption is carrying the deal.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: a rental lease-up, backward from the loan

Hypothetical again. A 200-unit rental building’s construction loan matures 18 months after completion. The permanent lender, as a matter of its own practice, wants the building 90 percent leased with three months of operating history at that level before it will fund.

  1. The finish line. 90 percent of 200 is 180 occupied units, reached three months before maturity, which is month 15.
  2. Net pace. 180 units in 15 months is 12 net leases a month.
  3. Gross pace. Some early tenants leave. If about one a month moves out during lease-up, you need 13 gross leases a month to net 12.
  4. Market test. New rental units in the submarket have absorbed about 1,000 a year, which is roughly 83 a month. Four other buildings are leasing up at the same time, five in total, so fair share is about 16.7 a month.
  5. Margin. 13 needed against 16.7 of fair share leaves a cushion of about 22 percent. That is a reasonable but not generous margin.

Now reverse the reverse. How slow can absorption get before you miss the date? You need 13 a month; fair share is 16.7. If market absorption fell by about 22 percent, fair share would drop to 13 and you would have no cushion at all. That is your break-even absorption: the market rate at which the deal just survives. Write it on the front page of the feasibility.

The sensitivity line

Put the condominium result into one line that a lender can read in ten seconds. Market new-unit sales at 35, 50 and 65 a month give required capture of about 23, 16 and 12 percent, against a fair share of 16.7. Only the middle and upper cases pass the fair share test. That line tells the reader immediately that the deal depends on the market staying at or above its three-year average. If the three-year average included the peak of a cycle, the deal is more fragile than it looks.

Do the same for the funnel. If visit-to-contract conversion falls from 15 to 10 percent, required visits rise from about 53 to 80 a month, and leads, at the same 2 percent, cannot be held where they were. Each conversion rate is an assumption, and each one should carry the name of the comparable launch it came from. An assumption with a source can be checked; an assumption with no source can only be believed.

Reading the result

Two numbers decide the go or no-go from this lesson: required capture against fair share, and break-even absorption against the market’s worst recent year. If the market’s worst year in the last decade was below your break-even, the deal survives only if this cycle is kinder than the last one. That is not a plan; it is a hope.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is using a market average from the top of a cycle as the base for every step, because each step inherits the optimism of the one before. A peak-year market figure, a strong-market conversion rate and an optimistic lead cost multiply together into a schedule that only works in the best year of the decade.

The control: run the backward calculation using the average across a full cycle and again using the worst recent year, and show both.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner also mixes units. Total condominium transactions include resales of older units, which are a different product competing on price, not location or finish. Comparing your new-unit pace with total transactions makes your capture rate look small and the deal look safe. Always compare like with like: new units against new units, at a similar price band, in the same submarket.

The beginner forgets the funnel. They confirm the market can absorb 8 units a month but never check whether their marketing budget can produce 400 leads a month. A sales schedule is only as real as the leads behind it.

Callback

In Week 17 you reverse engineered a deal from public information, working back from a sale price to the land value and rent it implied. This is the same discipline applied to time: from a required sell-out date back to the buyers per month it implies. Backward arithmetic exposes the load-bearing assumption.

Recap

Start from the outcome the financing needs, convert it to a monthly pace, a capture rate against fair share, a sales funnel and a marketing budget, and compute break-even absorption. Then test it against a full cycle and the worst recent year.

Next: JAX, The Room — defending an absorption forecast to an investment committee that wants it faster.
checklist: Start from the date the financing needs and convert it to a monthly pace.
Divide by comparable new-product absorption to get required capture.
Compare required capture with fair share of competing supply.
Convert the pace into visits and leads with stated conversion rates.
Check that the pro forma carries the marketing budget the leads require.
Compute break-even absorption and compare it with the worst recent year.
Run every step on a full-cycle average, not a peak-year figure.
head: Field checklist
speak: I work backward from the date the financing needs. On a hypothetical 160-unit condo that must sell out in 20 months, that is 8 units a month. Comparable new-unit sales average 50 a month, so I need 16 percent of the market, against a fair share of about 16.7 percent with six projects selling. No margin for being worse. At a 15 percent visit-to-contract rate I need about 53 visits a month, and at 2 percent of leads, 400 leads, which at 100 dollars each is 40,000 a month of marketing. For a 200-unit rental that must be 90 percent leased by month 15, I need 13 gross leases a month against a fair share of 16.7. If market absorption falls about 22 percent, my cushion is gone. That is break-even absorption, and I compare it with the worst year in the last cycle before I say go.
terms: Fair share — a project’s units divided by all competing new units in the same window; what it would capture if all projects were equal.
Sales funnel — the chain from enquiries to visits to contracts, each step with its own conversion rate.
Break-even absorption — the market absorption rate at which a project just meets its required schedule.

hostile.q: Your schedule needs 16 percent of the market. Why will you beat the five other projects?
hostile.a: I am not assuming I beat them; 16 percent is just under fair share, so the plan works with an average product at an average price. Where I expect to be better is shown separately as upside. The front page also shows break-even absorption, which is below the worst year of the last cycle.

title: Holding your absorption number when a partner wants it faster
summary: Feasibility studies are more often bent in meetings than broken by data. When a partner asks for faster absorption, translate the request into the real question, the return, show what the faster number implies, stay silent while they absorb it, and offer honest levers. Only new evidence moves the base case.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the hardest room for a feasibility study is not the one that doubts it. It is the one that wants it faster. Holding your absorption number against a partner who needs a better return is a test of evidence, structure and nerve.

Recall

Q. From this week, what is break-even absorption?

A. The market absorption rate at which the project just meets its required schedule; below it, the deal fails unless something else changes.

Q. From last week, why do supply pipelines swell late in a cycle?

A. Because approvals and financing granted in good times turn into construction starts that deliver years later, often into a weaker market.

Q. From contracts, when does an offer become a contract?

A. When it is accepted on its terms, with consideration where the law requires it and an intention to create legal relations. A counter-offer rejects the original offer.

Why this matters

JAX here. Most feasibility studies are not killed by bad data. They are bent by a meeting. Someone with money or authority says the absorption looks conservative, the room nods, the number moves, and the financing is sized on the new figure. You need to be able to hold a number without being rigid and change it only when the evidence changes.

The scene

This is a composite example. You are presenting a 150-unit rental project to the investment committee of a prospective equity partner. Your study shows lease-up at 10 units a month, 15 months to stabilisation. The partner’s managing director looks at the return, which is below their target, and says: “Ten a month feels conservative for this location. The broker told us 15. Can we run it at 15?”

The question behind the question

She is not really asking about absorption. She is asking whether there is a version of this deal that clears her committee’s hurdle. If you treat the question as an attack on your data, you will defend. If you treat it as a request to find a deal she can approve, you can help without lying. Your job is to separate the number you believe from the levers that could genuinely improve the return.

There is often a second question underneath: does this developer know the market, or are they reading from a consultant? A partner who is about to commit equity wants to see that you own the number. That is why the comparable leasing history matters more than the consultant’s name. When you can say which buildings leased at which pace, and why one was faster than another, you show judgement rather than reliance, and the conversation about absorption usually becomes much shorter.

Lines to say

  • “I can run it at 15. Before I do, here is what 15 means: a 30 percent capture of every qualifying household in the area for 10 months, against a fair share of 25 percent.”
  • “The last three comparable buildings leased at 8, 11 and 9 a month. Fifteen would be the best result in that set by a wide margin.”
  • “If the return is the issue, there are three levers that do not depend on the market being kind: the construction loan term, the unit mix, and the land price. I would rather move one of those.”
  • “I will show you the 15 case as upside, next to the base and downside, so the committee sees the range.”

Say that out loud now.

Lines never to say

  • “Sure, the consultant was probably being cautious.” You have just disowned your own evidence.
  • “Fifteen is impossible.” It is not impossible; it is unlikely, and you can show how unlikely.
  • “Whatever gets it through committee.” You have told the partner your numbers are negotiable, and they will remember it the first time the project misses.

When to stay silent

After you state the capture rate that 15 a month implies, stop talking. Let the managing director do the arithmetic. People believe the conclusion they reach themselves far more than the one you push. If she then says, “All right, show me the levers,” you have moved from a fight about data to a design conversation. The silence is where that happens.

Holding your state

Expect a flush of pressure when a senior person questions your number in front of others. Keep your voice at its normal pace and pitch, slow your next sentence slightly, and look at the data on the page rather than at her. That turns attention to the evidence instead of to the two of you. The one thing to protect is your willingness to say, “I do not believe 15.” Everything else is negotiable.

The likely outcome

In a good version of this meeting, the committee asks for the three cases, sees that 15 a month is a best case, and asks you to look at a longer loan term and a cheaper unit mix. The return moves a little, legitimately. In a bad version, the partner insists on 15 as the base case. Then the honest answer is that you are not the right partners for this deal, because your financing would be sized on a number you do not believe. Walking away from capital is cheaper than accepting it on a false absorption.

The follow-up

Within a day, send a short note. Thank the committee, restate the three cases with their absorption rates, list the levers you agreed to examine, and give the date you will return with results. Attach the comparable leasing history. The note fixes the record: if the partner later remembers that you agreed to 15, the paper shows otherwise. It also signals that you run a disciplined process, which is what an equity partner is really buying.

Then do the work you promised. If the longer loan term adds a point of return, show it. If the unit mix change does not help, say so plainly. A partner who sees you report a lever that failed learns to trust the ones that succeed.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting the base case drift under social pressure, so that the financing is sized on a number nobody would defend in writing. The control: the base case comes from evidence, every alternative is labelled upside or downside, and only new evidence moves the base.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner hears a challenge as a judgement on their competence and either caves to please or digs in to win. Both end the conversation. The professional translates the challenge into the real question, the return, and offers honest ways to address it.

Decision journals

This month’s thread is the decision journal, which you first met in Week 2. After a meeting like this one, write three lines before you sleep: the number you were pushed on, what you decided and why, and what result would prove you wrong. Date it. A year later, when the building is leased, you can compare your reasoning with what happened instead of with what you remember.

Over time the journal shows your patterns. You may find you concede under pressure from certain people, or that your downside cases are consistently too kind. That is the only reliable way to calibrate your judgement, because memory rewrites decisions to make you look wise.

Callback

In Week 6 you practised hostile questions: acknowledge, bridge, answer. This scene uses the same shape. Acknowledge that 15 is possible, bridge to what it implies, and answer with the evidence and the levers. And the fair share test from the first lesson of this week gives you the single figure that makes the bridge land.

Recap

When a partner wants faster absorption, translate the request into the real question, which is the return. Show what the faster number implies, stay silent while they absorb it, offer genuine levers, and keep every alternative labelled. Only evidence moves the base case.

Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap — the week on feasibility, with Cole in the Auditor’s Chair.
checklist: Translate a challenge to your number into the real question behind it.
State what the faster number implies as a capture rate against fair share.
Cite the leasing history of the last comparable buildings.
Offer levers that do not depend on the market: loan term, unit mix, land price.
Label every alternative as upside or downside, never as a new base.
Stay silent after stating the implication.
Write a three-line decision journal entry after the meeting.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a partner says my absorption looks conservative and asks me to run it faster, the real question is whether there is a version of the deal that clears their hurdle. So I say yes, I can run it, and here is what it means: 15 a month is a 30 percent capture against a fair share of 25, and the last three comparable buildings leased at 8, 11 and 9. Then I stop talking and let them do the arithmetic. If the return is the problem, I offer levers that do not depend on the market being kind: a longer loan term, a different unit mix, a lower land price. I show the faster case as upside beside the base and the downside. I never disown my own evidence, and I never say whatever gets it through committee. If they insist on the fast number as the base, we are the wrong partners for this deal.
terms: Investment committee — the group in an investing firm that approves or rejects deals against agreed criteria.
Base case — the set of assumptions you actually believe and would defend in writing.
Upside case — a labelled version with better-than-expected assumptions, shown to illustrate potential, not to size financing.

hostile.q: Our broker says 15 a month. Why should we trust your consultant over a broker who leases in this market every day?
hostile.a: You should trust neither on faith; trust the comparables. The last three buildings leased at 8, 11 and 9. If your broker can show a comparable that achieved 15, I will add it to the set and we can see what it does to the base case.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Feasibility week: quiz, recap and the Auditor’s Chair
summary: Six questions test demand, capture rate, fair share, Rule 28, the refinance gap and reliance letters. Cole’s Auditor’s Chair takes apart a hypothetical market study prepared by a conflicted leasing agent, and the boardroom drill explains feasibility in two minutes.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week turned feasibility into arithmetic and discipline: demand you can name, absorption as a rate, competing supply as a pipeline, and a go/no-go decision against criteria written in advance. Today you test it, and Cole reads a market study the way a hostile auditor would.

Recall

Q. From last week, what is the difference between a supply-led and a credit-led downturn?

A. A supply-led downturn comes from too many buildings delivering at once; a credit-led downturn comes from money becoming scarce or expensive. The worst cycles combine both.

Q. From the law and tax checkpoint, when should you challenge advice from a professional?

A. When the reasoning is not explained, the assumptions are not stated, or the advice conflicts with facts you know. Ask for the basis in writing; a good adviser welcomes it.

Q. From contracts, can silence count as acceptance?

A. Generally not, unless the parties have agreed otherwise or their past dealings make it reasonable. Do not rely on silence to form or vary a contract.

The six questions

Question 1. What makes a demand estimate usable? Answer: It names a price band, a geography and a time period, and counts households, buyers or guests with a reason, the income and a trigger to move. Population alone is not demand.

Question 2. A 150-unit building must lease up in 15 months in a market producing 50 qualifying households a month. What is the required capture rate? Answer: 150 divided by 15 is 10 a month; 10 divided by 50 is 20 percent.

Question 3. What is the fair share test? Answer: Compare required capture with your units divided by all competing new units in the window. Required capture above fair share means you must be better or cheaper to succeed.

Question 4. What was the root cause in Dubai, and what is Rule 28? Answer: Absorption was measured by contracts signed, not by occupiers, and long projects were funded with short money. Rule 28: count only end-user demand as absorption, track the investor share of every pre-sale, and never fund a long build with money that comes due before the building can pay it back.

Question 5. Why does a slow lease-up threaten the refinance? Answer: The permanent lender sizes the loan on actual net operating income at the refinance date. Low occupancy means low income, a smaller maximum loan, and a gap on the construction loan maturity date.

Question 6. What is a reliance letter, and when do you negotiate it? Answer: An agreement letting a named third party, such as a lender, rely on a consultant’s report, usually on the original terms and liability limits. Negotiate it before the report is delivered.

Recap

Feasibility is a test designed to fail the deal. Demand must be named and priced. Absorption is a monthly rate, converted into a required capture rate and tested against fair share of the full pipeline. Slow absorption costs carry and time, and threatens the refinance. Studies are advice with legal edges. Work backward from the date the financing needs to find break-even absorption, and hold the base case in the room until evidence moves it.

Say that out loud now.

Auditor’s Chair

This is week 28, so the Red Pen becomes Cole’s Auditor’s Chair. Read this hypothetical extract from a market study summary as a hostile auditor would: assume every claim must be proved.

Market Study Summary, hypothetical. Demand: the city population of 480,000 is growing strongly, supporting robust demand for new rental housing. Absorption: the project is expected to lease 15 units per month, consistent with strong market conditions. Competition: two comparable buildings are currently operating, both over 95 percent leased. Conclusion: the market can comfortably support the 150-unit project. Prepared for the developer by its leasing agent, whose fee is payable on project approval. Data current to the date of this report.

The defects, read with an auditor’s suspicion:

  1. Demand is population, not demand. No price band, no geography, no number of qualifying households, and an adjective, “robust”, in place of a figure.
  2. Absorption has no basis. Fifteen a month is asserted, not derived. There is no capture rate and no comparable leasing history.
  3. Competition counts only what is open. Two operating buildings at 95 percent say nothing about the pipeline under construction, approved or applied for.
  4. No downside case. A single number with “comfortably” attached.
  5. Conflict of interest. The author is the leasing agent, paid only if the project is approved. That does not make the report wrong, but it removes its independence and must be disclosed.
  6. No data date. “Current to the date of this report” with no date is not a date.
  7. No reliance terms. Nothing says who may rely on it, so a lender cannot.

The auditor’s verdict: this document cannot support a go decision. Commission an independent study with a named demand estimate, a derived absorption rate, a pipeline schedule, a downside case and reliance terms.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week to a board in two minutes. Set a timer, speak, then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: “Before we buy land, we test whether anyone will pay for what we build, fast enough to repay the loan. We name demand as a price band, an area and a time period. We turn absorption into units per month and a capture rate, and test it against our fair share of every competing project in the pipeline, not just what is open today. We work backward from the date our financing needs to find break-even absorption, and compare it with the worst year of the last cycle. Slow absorption costs us carry and time, and on a rental it shrinks the loan available at refinance, so our loan term, extensions and reserves are sized to the slow case. We go only if the project passes kill criteria we signed before the land deposit went hard. And we count only end-user demand, because sales to people planning to resell disappear when credit does.”

One exercise for this week

Choose any submarket you know, with no project attached. List every rental or condominium building under construction, approved or applied for, with unit counts and expected delivery dates, using public planning records and news. Then find the leasing or sales pace of the last three buildings that opened there. You now have a pipeline schedule and a reference class. Keep it updated quarterly. When a real site comes along, half of your feasibility will already be done, and done by someone with nothing to gain from the answer.

Notice what happens to your view of the market as you do this. Most people who build the pipeline list for the first time find more supply coming than they expected, because planning applications and approvals are far less visible than cranes.

Callback

In Week 13 you met estimate classes for cost: the earlier the estimate, the wider its range. Absorption deserves the same humility, and it deserves the same discipline of narrowing. As you move from site search to land agreement to financing, the absorption range should tighten because you have gathered evidence, not because you have grown attached. An early feasibility number is a range, and the go/no-go gate tests the bad end of it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is believing your own feasibility because you wrote it. The control is independence and kill criteria, in that order.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner also treats feasibility as a document produced once. The professional treats it as a living file, updated at every gate with new pipeline data, new comparables and new interest rates, so the go/no-go decision at each gate is made on current facts.

The beginner reads a confident study and feels reassured. The professional reads it and looks for the number that was asserted rather than derived.

Next: Remi, First Principles — asset types, and how a rental, a condominium and a hotel each earn their money.
checklist: What makes a demand estimate usable?
A 150-unit building must lease up in 15 months in a market producing 50 qualifying households a month. What is the required capture rate?
What is the fair share test?
What was the root cause in Dubai, and what is Rule 28?
Why does a slow lease-up threaten the refinance?
What is a reliance letter, and when do you negotiate it?
head: The six questions
speak: This week I learned that feasibility is a test designed to kill the deal. Demand must be named as a price band, an area and a period. Absorption is a monthly rate, which becomes a required capture rate; I test it against my fair share of the whole pipeline. Dubai taught me to count only end-user demand, because buyers planning to resell vanish with credit. Slow absorption costs carry and time, and on a rental it shrinks the take-out loan, so I size the loan term, extensions and reserves to the slow case. A market study is advice: the engagement letter decides who may rely on it, and any forecast I pass on carries its downside and assumptions. I work backward from the date my financing needs to break-even absorption, compare it with the worst year of the last cycle, and decide against kill criteria I signed before the land money went hard.
terms: Kill criteria — specific, pre-written results that stop a project at a go/no-go gate.
Independence — the absence of any interest in the outcome on the part of the person giving an opinion.
Data date — the date to which the information in a study is current.

hostile.q: Your market study was written by your leasing agent. Why is it not just a sales pitch?
hostile.a: It may be, which is why it is not our decision document. We commissioned an independent study with a derived absorption rate, a pipeline schedule, a downside case and reliance terms for the lender, and the agent’s view is shown separately as a market opinion with its conflict disclosed.
